title: Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity
subfield: Banking / Financial Intermediation / Theory of Financial Crises
datasets: None (purely theoretical paper; no data, calibration, or simulation)
research_question: Can a contract between a bank and ex ante identical depositors who face privately observed, non-verifiable heterogeneity in the timing of consumption needs implement full-information-optimal risk sharing as an equilibrium, and is that implementation unique or does it necessarily coexist with a self-fulfilling bank-run equilibrium?
main_finding: A demand-deposit contract with sequential service can implement optimal risk sharing as one equilibrium, but the identical contract admits a strictly worse run equilibrium for any early-withdrawal value above the liquidation value of the bank's assets; suspension of convertibility restores uniqueness only when withdrawal demand is deterministic, no sequential-service contract can achieve full efficiency once it is stochastic (Proposition 1), and government deposit insurance financed by ex post taxation can implement the unconstrained optimum uniquely because taxation is not bound by the order of the withdrawal queue (Proposition 2).
research_gaps: No theory of what triggers coordination on the run equilibrium versus the good one (sunspot-selection is left exogenous)
Riskless technology precludes any role for genuine insolvency, so the panic-versus-fundamentals distinction cannot be addressed
Proposition 2's efficiency result depends on costless, unconstrained ex post taxation, which does not match how deposit insurance is actually financed
Single representative bank with no interbank market or contagion channel
research_ideas: Test whether uninsured deposit concentration predicts run severity in the 2023 U.S. regional-bank episode using FDIC call report data
Test whether digital/instant withdrawal technology has weakened the sequential-service constraint's empirical bite relative to pre-digital banking
Apply the Goldstein-Pauzner global-games refinement to estimate a structural run-probability function against 2023 bank failure data
Test the model's insurance-versus-no-insurance comparative static using money market fund runs in 2008 and 2020
Apply the model's multiple-equilibrium structure to stablecoin de-pegging and redemption episodes using on-chain data

title: The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities
methods: Parabolic Partial Differential Equation Solution (Heat-Equation Analogy)
datasets: None (theoretical paper; own empirical test summarized only by reference to Black and Scholes 1972)
research_question: Can a European call option be valued as a function solely of the underlying stock price, the exercise price, time to maturity, the risk-free rate, and the stock's variance rate, with the free parameters of earlier warrant-pricing formulas pinned down by a no-arbitrage condition rather than by an assumed, unobservable investor risk preference or discount rate?
main_finding: A continuously rebalanced, riskless hedge of the stock against the option, combined with the requirement that a riskless position earn the risk-free rate, yields a partial differential equation mathematically identical to the heat-transfer equation; its closed-form solution, w(x,t) = xN(d1) - c*e^{-r(t*-t)}N(d2), depends on no unobservable risk-preference parameter, is independently reproduced via the capital asset pricing model, extends to European puts through put-call parity, and, under a reinterpretation of variables, prices corporate equity and risky debt as options on a levered firm's assets.
research_gaps: No closed-form solution is provided for American put options, which the paper explicitly flags as unsolved
The cost and risk of discrete (non-continuous) rebalancing relative to the idealized continuous hedge is acknowledged but never bounded or quantified
The constant-variance-rate assumption, later shown empirically false for equity index options after the 1987 crash, underlies the closed-form solution itself and is not relaxed anywhere in the paper
The corporate-liabilities application (equity and debt as options on firm value) is asserted qualitatively but never tested against a numerical example or market data within the paper
research_ideas: Decompose the post-1987 S&P 500 implied-volatility skew into jump risk (Merton 1976) versus stochastic-volatility risk (Heston 1993) versus residual mispricing, using the original constant-variance model as the explicit null hypothesis
Test the Merton (1974) option-theoretic credit spread implied by the paper's corporate-liabilities extension against realized corporate default and recovery data
Bound the dollar cost and hedging error of discrete delta-rebalancing relative to the paper's idealized continuous hedge using high-frequency option and underlying data
Test whether the constant-known-interest-rate assumption caused material mispricing of long-dated warrants during the high-rate-volatility period of the early 1980s
Apply the equity-as-a-call-option-on-assets framework to over-collateralized crypto stablecoins to price de-pegging risk as a new class of contingent corporate-style liability

title: Theory of the Firm: Managerial Behavior, Agency Costs and Ownership Structure
subfield: Corporate Finance / Theory of the Firm / Agency Theory
datasets: None (purely theoretical paper; no data, calibration, or simulation)
research_question: Given an entrepreneur-manager with personal wealth below the investment outlay required to exploit a profitable project, and given that only outside equity and limited-liability debt can be issued, what mixture of inside equity, outside equity, and debt minimizes the sum of the agency costs generated by outside equity (perquisite consumption and under-investment) and by debt (risk-shifting, monitoring, bonding, and bankruptcy costs)?
main_finding: A rational, competitive market for outside claims prices anticipated managerial opportunism into the sale price of both equity and debt, so the manager alone bears the full capitalized agency cost of the ownership structure he chooses; selling outside equity induces perquisite consumption and an investment scale strictly below the value-maximizing level (Section 3.2), selling debt creates a risk-shifting incentive formalized via the Black-Scholes mapping of equity to a call option on firm value, under which equity value can rise even as total firm value falls because bondholders absorb a disproportionate share of the loss (equation 6), and the resulting ownership structure is the interior mixture of debt and outside equity that minimizes the sum of the two cost schedules.
research_gaps: No formal proof of existence or uniqueness of the interior optimal debt-equity mix under general, non-additively-separable agency-cost functions (Kürsten, 1995, shows separability fails once managerial ownership and risky debt interact)
No treatment of multi-period reputation effects; the single production-financing decision assumption (P.6) rules out repeat-issuer bonding-cost reductions
No treatment of the agency costs of free cash flow retained inside a mature firm absent new outside financing, later addressed by Jensen (1986)
No calibration of the model's implied magnitude of agency costs against directly measured proxies such as covenant intensity or governance scores
research_ideas: Test whether the marginal agency cost of debt varies with managerial ownership concentration using DealScan covenant data merged with private-equity sponsor stakes, directly testing the additive-separability assumption of the Section 5 synthesis
Test the Section 3.2 under-investment prediction in founder-controlled dual-class technology IPOs where cash-flow and voting rights are observably separated
Re-test the paper's regulated-industry leverage prediction against a fifty-year Compustat panel spanning utility and banking deregulation episodes
Structurally estimate the manager's utility and monitoring-cost primitives against the joint distribution of managerial ownership, leverage, and covenant intensity in Compustat/ExecuComp data
Test the risk-shifting mechanism in DeFi lending protocol governance votes, exploiting close-vote regression discontinuities as a source of quasi-random variation in risk-parameter changes

title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds
datasets: Ibbotson Associates government and corporate bond returns
research_question: Do portfolios mimicking size, book-to-market equity, and term-structure/default risk capture common variation in U.S. stock and bond returns, and do their average premiums explain the cross-section of average returns on both asset classes?
main_finding: A market factor, SMB, and HML jointly capture the great majority of common variation in twenty-five size-book-to-market stock portfolios and leave three-factor intercepts close to zero (only 2 of 25 exceed 0.2%/month, 16 of 25 within 0.1%), while TERM and DEF dominate common variation in bond returns and, once the market factor is orthogonalized, are shown to be common to stock returns as well; DEF's strong loadings but near-zero average premium demonstrate that capturing common variation and carrying a priced risk premium are logically distinct properties.
research_gaps: No identification of the economic state variable(s) SMB and HML proxy for
SMB and HML are constructed from and tested on the same sample already known to predict average returns (in-sample factor construction)
E/P and D/P robustness portfolios are announced but their results were not accessible in the retrieved primary text
No formal treatment of generated-regressor standard-error inflation in the second-stage average-return tests
research_ideas: Replicate the three-factor tests with full-universe rather than NYSE-only size/BE-ME breakpoints over 1963-2025
Test whether HML factor loadings predict subsequent firm-level default and downgrade outcomes, as a direct proxy for a distress-risk state variable
Re-test the Chen-Roll-Ross DEF loading/price-of-risk dissociation out of sample using a longer corporate bond history
Add a momentum factor to the original 25 test assets and sample window to see whether it explains the two largest residual three-factor intercepts
Re-run a Daniel-Titman characteristics-versus-covariances test with modern nonparametric methods, split before and after the factors became widely known

title: Efficient Capital Markets: A Review of Theory and Empirical Work
subfield: Asset Pricing / Efficient Markets Hypothesis / Financial Econometrics
datasets: 30 DJIA stocks, daily prices, c. late 1957-September 1962 (Fama 1965)
261 firms, annual earnings announcements, 1946-1966 (Ball and Brown 1968)
research_question: Does the equilibrium expected return on a security, conditioned on progressively larger information sets (historical prices, all public information, and all information including that held monopolistically), fully absorb that information such that no trading rule conditioned on the corresponding set can generate expected profit in excess of the assumed equilibrium model?
main_finding: Market efficiency is empirically testable only when paired with an assumed equilibrium expected-return model, yielding a fair-game property that nests the submartingale and, as a stronger special case, the random walk; across weak-form (serial correlation, filter rules), semi-strong-form (the FFJR stock-split event study, Ball-Brown earnings announcements), and strong-form (Jensen's mutual-fund performance) tests, dependence is either statistically negligible or too small to survive realistic transaction costs, with specialists (and, via Scholes's evidence, corporate insiders) as the clear documented exceptions; the paper explicitly states, in its own text, what would later be called the joint-hypothesis problem.
research_gaps: No direct test of the Sharpe-Lintner CAPM was available at time of writing; conclusions rest on an untested single-index market-model proxy
No decision-theoretic or information-economics microfoundation for who bears the cost of gathering information and why prices should reflect it
Strong-form evidentiary base is narrow (specialists, one thesis-level insider inference, one mutual-fund study) relative to the sweeping conclusion drawn
No discussion of survivorship bias in any of the samples reviewed (30 surviving DJIA stocks, 940 realized splits, 115 surviving funds)
research_ideas: Decompose Lo-MacKinlay-style weak-form dependence into risk-based and genuinely anomalous components using modern multifactor models, directly quantifying Fama's own joint-hypothesis wedge
Replicate the Niederhoffer-Osborne transaction-level reversal pattern using modern limit-order-book equity and crypto data to test whether it remains non-exploitable net of costs

Use machine-learning models trained only on public information (filings, news, alternative data) as a continuous-time analogue to Fama's discrete semi-strong event studies, measuring signal decay speed
Apply the weak/semi-strong/strong-form taxonomy to cryptocurrency markets to test whether Fama's conclusions are specific to 1960s U.S. equity institutions or generalize to organized markets broadly
Re-audit the FFJR event-study methodology with modern robust and clustered inference and a multifactor benchmark instead of the single-index market model

title: Noise Trader Risk in Financial Markets
subfield: Behavioral Finance / Limits to Arbitrage / Asset Pricing
datasets: None (theoretical paper; empirical anomalies discussed are drawn from citations to independent studies, not estimated by the authors)
research_question: Can the unpredictability of irrational noise traders' future beliefs, as distinct from any risk in an asset's fundamentals, constitute a priced risk that limits risk-averse, short-horizon arbitrageurs enough to sustain a persistent gap between price and fundamental value, and can noise traders earn a higher expected return than the arbitrageurs who trade against them?
main_finding: In a two-asset overlapping-generations model purged of all fundamental risk, the equilibrium price of the risky asset (eq. 12) sits below its riskless substitute purely because of noise trader risk, and the expected return gap between noise traders and sophisticated investors (eq. 18) decomposes into four offsetting effects (hold more, price pressure, Friedman, create space) that make the gap positive only over an interior range of average noise-trader bullishness; whether the noise-trader population share survives in the long run under an imitation dynamic depends on whether fundamental risk is present and on whether imitation is based on realized returns (survives) or realized utility (does not survive).
research_gaps: No account of why noise traders hold the beliefs they hold or why the population share μ is fixed rather than an equilibrium object
No calibration of ρ*, σ²ρ, or μ against any real market, so the model is an existence result rather than a quantitative account of any anomaly's magnitude
No test discriminating the noise-trader-risk mechanism from Grossman-Stiglitz rational, privately-informed heterogeneous-agent explanations of the same reduced-form patterns
The long-run survival of noise traders is reversed under an equally plausible utility-based imitation rule, so the result is imitation-rule-dependent rather than structural
research_ideas: Test the non-monotonic, interior-maximum shape of the noise trader return-gap prediction (eq. 18) directly against retail brokerage trading records sorted by measured sentiment
Structurally estimate μ, ρ*, and σ²ρ from closed-end fund discount time series using simulated method of moments
Test the model's horizon-lengthening comparative static using staggered pension-fund manager evaluation-frequency reforms as a natural experiment
Construct information-free sentiment shocks (in the spirit of Roll 1984) to discriminate the noise-trader-risk mechanism from rational private-information explanations
Extend the closed-end fund discount application to on-chain single-asset crypto trust products, using wallet-level data as a direct proxy for the noise-trader population share

title: On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets
subfield: Theory of Market Efficiency / Information Economics / Noisy Rational Expectations Equilibrium
methods: Conditional Moment Calculation Under Joint Normality
Comparative Statics via Closed-Form Equilibrium Condition
datasets: None (purely theoretical paper; no data, calibration, or simulation)
research_question: In an economy where a costly private signal about a risky asset's payoff can be acquired by any trader and price clears the market competitively, does an equilibrium fraction of informed traders and an associated price function exist, and can that equilibrium ever coincide with price revealing the informed traders' signal perfectly?
main_finding: A fraction lambda of traders acquires costly information in a unique equilibrium (Theorem 3) in which price is a linear, noisy aggregator of their signal (Theorem 1); equilibrium price informativeness depends only on information cost, signal quality, and risk aversion, and is invariant to the level of supply noise, which is instead absorbed by an offsetting change in lambda (Theorem 4); and a competitive equilibrium fails to exist at the two limits that would make price fully revealing -- zero noise or costlessly perfect information (Theorem 5) -- because full revelation eliminates the private return to information that sustains it.
research_gaps: No general proof of the seven Section I conjectures outside the CARA-normal example
No welfare analysis of the equilibrium, explicitly deferred by the authors to future work
Heterogeneous endowments excluded by assumption (footnote 9), leaving the 'vanishing trade' resolution of Theorem 6 untested against a non-informational source of trade
No treatment of strategic, price-impact-aware informed traders; the nonexistence result is specific to price-taking behavior, as Kyle (1985) later shows
research_ideas: Test Theorem 4's compensating-adjustment prediction using a staggered disclosure-cost shock (e.g., structured-data filing mandates) against analyst/institutional coverage and price-informativeness data
Re-derive the model with a finite number of Kyle-style strategic informed traders to isolate whether price-taking is what drives the nonexistence result
Re-derive Theorems 1-6 with heterogeneous endowments restored to test whether trading volume still collapses to zero at the model's degenerate limits
Use options-market information share as an empirical proxy for lambda to test Theorem 4's comparative statics around earnings announcements
Test whether the Grossman-Stiglitz mechanism, reinterpreted around the cost of interpreting rather than observing data, extends to fully transparent on-chain decentralized-exchange markets
